key_terms.meaning: 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F): finite states, input alphabet, tape alphabet, transition function, start state, blank symbol, accepting states.
Unbounded one-dimensional array of cells; each cell holds one symbol from Γ.
Points to one tape cell; reads its symbol, writes a symbol, then moves L or R.
The state q ∈ Q that decides the next move from the scanned tape symbol.
δ: Q×Γ → Q×Γ×{L,R}; maps current state and read symbol to new state, written symbol, head move.
Graph with states as nodes and arrows q → p labelled a/b,R when δ(q,a)=(p,b,R).
Snapshot written αqβ: α is tape left of head, q is current state, β is tape from head to right end.
I ⊢ J means ID I becomes ID J in one move; ⊢* means zero or more moves.
q0w: start state q0 with head on the first symbol of input w.
An ID whose state is in F; reaching it means the TM accepts the input.
L(M) = {w ∈ Σ* : q0w ⊢* α qf β for some qf ∈ F}.
A language accepted by some TM; also called Turing-recognizable.
A language accepted by a TM that halts on every input; also called recursive.
Integer n is written as n copies of 1; zero is written as no 1s in the usual convention.
A TM with k tapes and k heads; one move reads all k scanned symbols and updates all tapes.
δ returns a finite set of possible moves; the NTM accepts if some branch reaches an accepting state.
A TM U that reads a code ⟨M,w⟩ and simulates M on w, accepting iff M accepts w.
Every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine.
Encoding bounded information, such as the last symbol or a small counter, in state names instead of tape cells.

takeaways: A Turing machine is a finite control with one read/write head on an unbounded tape; one move depends on the state and the scanned symbol.
An instantaneous description αqβ records the whole tape, the state and the head position, so a run is a sequence of IDs linked by ⊢.
A TM accepts a string when its run reaches an accepting state; L(M) is the set of all such strings.
TMs are designed by small state routines, and integer functions are computed using unary tape codes.
Multitape and nondeterministic TMs are convenient variants; they recognize the same languages as the single-tape model.
A universal TM reads a coded description of any TM and simulates it, so one fixed machine can run many programs.
The Church-Turing thesis identifies TM computability with effective computability; it is a thesis, not a theorem.
Storing bounded facts in state names can simplify designs and reduce tape work.

glossary.def: A finite nonempty set of symbols.
The set of symbols allowed in input strings; usually Σ ⊆ Γ.
The set of all symbols a tape cell may hold, including the blank symbol B.
A special tape symbol for empty cells; it is usually not in Σ.
The finite set of control states of a Turing machine.
The state of the machine before any move.
The set of states that make the machine accept; F ⊆ Q.
The rule giving the next state, written symbol and head move.
A complete snapshot of tape contents, state and head position.
A string αqβ that writes a configuration compactly.
The one-step move relation between instantaneous descriptions.
A sequence of instantaneous descriptions linked by yields.
The machine stops because no transition applies or because it enters an accepting or rejecting state.
A run reaches a state in F.
A run halts in a nonaccepting state.
A language accepted by a Turing machine that halts on every input.
A language accepted by some Turing machine; the machine may loop on nonmembers.
Writing integer n as n copies of the symbol 1.
A Turing machine with several tapes and one head per tape.
A Turing machine whose transition function returns a set of possible moves.
A Turing machine that simulates any coded Turing machine on a coded input.
A finite string that encodes a machine M and an input string w.
A finite, mechanical, step-by-step method that can be followed without insight.
One machine imitating the step-by-step behaviour of another.
Remembering a bounded amount of data in state names rather than on the tape.
